newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew upbeat on Asia, Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew upbeat on Asia, Hong Kong.

text.p: Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew has said changing U.S. attitudes toward China should herald more investment confidence and economic growth for Asia.

Lee, now Senior Minister after 31 years as prime minister, said the outlook for Asia had "changed radically" since tension in the Taiwan Straits last year when U.S. warships were sent there during Chinese military exercises off Taiwan.
"China and America have both looked over the cliff and realised that too much was at stake," Lee said in a lunar new year speech on Monday and distributed on Tuesday.
He said that however strongly Americans believed they could convert the world to their standards of human rights and democracy, they had decided to allow China time to change.
"I believe that broader and deeper economic links with the U.S. will change China's economy, and with it the Chinese people, as has already been happening," Lee said.
He cited several events he said reflected a more pragmatic U.S. approach, such as President Bill Clinton's promise of a "deeper engagement with China" in his second term.
"The whole of Asia looks forward to a deep engagement between the U.S. and China covering economic, strategic and security issues," Lee said.
He also urged China to consider pressure on Clinton from anti-China critics in Congress, media and pro-Taiwan lobbyists.
"China will have to take these into account and accommodate Clinton's difficulties if Clinton is not to be swayed from his policy," Lee said.

He said if such a policy prevailed over the next four years, then economic ties between the two countries would be "so broad, so deep and so mutually beneficial," the next U.S. administration could not reverse it.
Lee said he also believed the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 would make little difference to the British colony.
"Its economy will continue to be buoyant," Lee said.

"I have not said this to boost Hong Kong's morale and confidence," he said "The (Singapore) Government Investment Corporation has invested, and is continuing to invest, a few billion dollars in Hong Kong.".
Hong Kong would prosper provided its people mind Hong Kong's business and not China's politics, Lee said.
"Hong Kong's leaders and people have to make up their minds whether they want to prosper under one country, two systems, or to engage China in human rights and democracy," he said.
Lee said Hong Kong needed a strong-minded and firm chief executive supported by an incorrupt and efficient civil service.

"To preserve the virtues of the British system; the rule of law and the sanctity of contracts, fair commercial practices, a level playing-field between all players whether they be well connected insiders or unconnected outsiders, and transparency and accountability in all decision-making," Lee added.
